title: Solutions: Concentration Terms and Raoult's Law
subcategory: Solutions — Concentration Units, Raoult's Law, Ideal and Non-Ideal Solutions

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Solutions

summary: Solution concentration can be expressed in several ways (molarity, molality, mole fraction, etc.), each with different temperature-dependence; Raoult's law predicts vapour pressure lowering for ideal solutions, with deviations pointing to specific intermolecular interaction changes.
explanation: Molarity (mol solute per litre of SOLUTION) is temperature-dependent because solution volume expands/contracts with temperature; molality (mol solute per kg of SOLVENT) and mole fraction (mol of a component / total mol of all components) are both temperature-INDEPENDENT, since they're based on mass or mole ratios rather than volume — this is exactly why molality is preferred for colligative property calculations across a temperature range. Raoult's law states that for an ideal solution, the partial vapour pressure of each volatile component is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution: pA = pA° × xA, where pA° is the vapour pressure of pure A. For a two-component ideal solution, total vapour pressure = pA° xA + pB° xB (a straight-line relationship with composition). An IDEAL solution obeys Raoult's law across the full composition range, requires solute-solvent interactions to be essentially identical in strength to solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions, and has ΔHmixing = 0 and ΔVmixing = 0 (e.g., benzene + toluene, very similar molecules). Non-ideal solutions show deviations: POSITIVE deviation occurs when solute-solvent interactions are WEAKER than the pure-component interactions (molecules escape more easily than expected, so observed vapour pressure > Raoult's law prediction) — e.g., ethanol + acetone. NEGATIVE deviation occurs when solute-solvent interactions are STRONGER (e.g., new hydrogen bonding forms between unlike molecules), so observed vapour pressure < Raoult's law prediction — e.g., chloroform + acetone. Certain non-ideal mixtures with extreme deviation form an azeotrope — a mixture that boils at a constant temperature and distills over WITHOUT any change in composition, meaning it cannot be separated further by simple fractional distillation.
commonMisconceptions: Using molarity interchangeably with molality in colligative property/temperature-dependent calculations — molarity changes with temperature (due to volume changes) while molality does not, making them non-interchangeable whenever temperature varies.

Assuming positive deviation from Raoult's law means STRONGER intermolecular attraction between different components — it is actually the reverse: positive deviation signals WEAKER unlike-molecule interactions (compared to like-molecule interactions), letting molecules escape into vapour more easily than ideally predicted.

Believing an azeotrope is a pure compound — it is a specific-composition MIXTURE that simply happens to boil at one constant temperature without changing its composition on boiling, and can still, in principle, be separated by other (non-distillation) methods.
examples: A mixture of ethanol and water forms a well-known azeotrope (~95.6% ethanol) that ordinary fractional distillation cannot concentrate further.
Benzene and toluene, being structurally very similar, form a nearly ideal solution obeying Raoult's law closely across the whole composition range.
genZNote: Raoult's law: ideal solutions play by the rules, real solutions deviate depending on who's vibing with whom.
